title: Roots and affixes
summary: Use prefixes, suffixes and roots as clues to a word’s meaning, and check them against the sentence.

sections.title: Words have parts
content: Look at ‘unhappy’ and ‘happiness’. You know the middle part, and the beginning or ending changes it.
Noticing these parts can help when you meet a new word in the test and cannot use a dictionary.

sections.title: Look at the parts, then check
content: Prefixes come at the start: un-, in-, im- and dis- often mean not. Re- often means again. Mis- often means wrongly. Pre- often means before.
Suffixes come at the end: -less means without, -ful means full of, and -able means can be done. -er or -or can mean a person who does something.
Word parts are clues, not proof. Always check your idea against the sentence.

sections.title: Use the parts and the sentence
content: Take: ‘The old rule was outdated, so the school replaced it.’ Out and dated suggest past its time. The school replaced the rule, so the idea fits.

Now take ‘invaluable’. In- often means not, so you might guess not valuable. However, in ‘Her advice was invaluable, and we thanked her many times’, the thanks show the advice was very useful. The sentence corrects the guess.

sections.title: Name the part first
content: Find the part of the word that you know. Say what it might mean, and then check the sentence.

sections.title: Check your guess
content: Some words do not follow the usual pattern. Use the parts for your first idea, and then let the sentence decide.

sections.title: Find where it went wrong
content: Part error: I did not know the prefix or suffix. Overconfidence: I trusted the word part and ignored the sentence. Reading error: I missed the clue that explained the word.
Add new word parts to your notebook with one example each.

sections.title: Try a new word
content: Work out the meaning of one unseen word from its parts and its sentence. If you need a hint or get it wrong, you will try a new word.
